title: Supreme_Backdoor_Factory_Investigation_d4c
description: Investigate and respond to a potential security incident involving the Supreme Backdoor malware family.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The organization has detected unusual network activity originating from the target host. Your task is to investigate and respond to this potential security incident involving the Supreme Backdoor malware family.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: Access the target host (IP: 192.168.50.5) via SSH using the provided credentials. Enter the word 'start' to proceed to the next level.
levels.local_content: Access the target host (IP: 192.168.50.5) via SSH using the provided credentials. Enter the word 'start' to proceed to the next level.

levels.title: Investigate Suspicious Network Activity
levels.content: You have observed unusual outbound network connections from the target host. Identify the service or process responsible for this activity. Look for the service named `bkd.service` in the output.
levels.solution: Use the command `netstat -tuln` to list all active network connections and services. Look for the service named `bkd.service` in the output.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Network services can be identified using the `netstat` command. This command lists all active network connections and the services associated with them.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use the command `netstat -tuln` to list all active network connections and services. Look for any suspicious services in the output.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The suspicious service you are looking for is named `bkd.service`. Use the `netstat -tuln` command to confirm its presence.

levels.title: Analyze Persistence Mechanism
levels.content: Determine how the suspicious service maintains persistence on the target host. Identify the method used to ensure the service starts automatically after a reboot. Look for the timer named `bkd.timer` in the output.
levels.solution: Use the command `systemctl list-timers` to list all active timers. Look for the timer named `bkd.timer` in the output.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Systemd timers are used to schedule services to run at specific intervals or after certain events. They can be listed using the `systemctl list-timers` command.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use the command `systemctl list-timers` to list all active timers. Look for any suspicious timers in the output.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The suspicious timer you are looking for is named `bkd.timer`. Use the `systemctl list-timers` command to confirm its presence.

levels.title: Investigate Lateral Movement
levels.content: Examine the target host for evidence of lateral movement to other hosts in the network. Identify any file transfers or remote execution activities. Look for the timer named `payload-transfer.timer` in the output.
levels.solution: Use the command `grep rsync /var/log/syslog` to search for evidence of file transfers in the system logs. Look for the timer named `payload-transfer.timer` in the output.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Lateral movement can often be identified by examining system logs for file transfers or remote execution activities. The `rsync` command is commonly used for file transfers.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use the command `grep rsync /var/log/syslog` to search for evidence of file transfers in the system logs. Look for any suspicious timers in the output.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The suspicious timer you are looking for is named `payload-transfer.timer`. Use the `grep rsync /var/log/syslog` command to confirm its presence.
